B.explanation: This copies the shape of the $v$-$t$ graph, but the gradient of $s$ must equal $v$, so $s$ cannot have maximum gradient at $t = 0$ where $v = 0$.

Connect $s$ to $v$ using gradient: the gradient of an $s$-$t$ graph equals $v$, so $s$ must start flat, get steepest when $v$ is largest, and be flat again where $v = 0$.

Compare areas under the $v$-$t$ graph: the positive area in the first half builds up $s$, and the equal negative area in the second half removes it, so $s$ must rise to a maximum then fall back to zero.
walkthrough: Identify the given $v$-$t$ information: at $t = 0$, $v = 0$; $v > 0$ for the first half; $v = 0$ at the middle; $v < 0$ for the second half; $v = 0$ again at $t = T$.
State the governing rules: gradient of displacement-time equals velocity, $v = ds/dt$, and change in $s$ equals area under the $v$-$t$ graph.

In the first half $v$ is positive, so $s$ must increase from $0$. Because $v$ starts at zero, the $s$-$t$ graph starts with zero gradient, then steepens as $v$ grows and flattens as $v$ falls back to zero.
At the middle time $v = 0$, so the $s$-$t$ gradient is zero and $s$ reaches its maximum value equal to the positive area under $v$.
In the second half $v$ is negative, so $s$ must decrease. The negative area has the same magnitude as the positive area, so $s$ falls smoothly back to zero at $t = T$.
Only the graph that starts flat at the origin, rises to one smooth maximum, then falls smoothly back to zero at $T$ matches this. This is option A.
